###         Step 4.1: Load the librares and data

```{r}
# Load the tidyverse collection of packages
# If R says "there is no package called 'tidyverse'", run this once in the console to install the package:

# install.package("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```


### Import and read datasets
```{r}
# Store each dataset file in a variable so it is easy to change in one place
population_path <- "world_population.csv"
co2_path <- "CO2_emission.csv"

# Read each CSV into its own tibble (a tidier kind of data frame)
world_population <- read_csv(population_path)
co2_emisions <- read_csv(co2_path)
```
###   Step 4.2(part1): Inspect the population data, duplicates, missing values

### Confirm if datasets loading worked successfully
```{r}
# Dimensions: number of rows and columns
dim(world_population)
dim(co2_emisions)

# Column names, data types and a preview of values
glimpse(world_population)
glimpse(co2_emisions)
```

###   1. Variable names, shape and data types
#           *** names(): lists the column names
#           *** dim() / nrow() /ncol(): the shape (rows, columns)
#           *** supply(df, class): applies class() to every column to show its             data type

```{r}

# column names of the population dataset
names(world_population)

# Shape of the dataset: number of rows and columns
cat("Rows:", nrow(world_population), "\n")
cat("Columns:", ncol(world_population), "\n")

# Data type of each column
sapply(world_population, class)
```
#  2. Top 5 and bottom 10 rows
#       head(x, n): first n rows. *** tail(x, n): last n rows.

```{r}
# First 5 rows
head(world_population, n=5)

# Last 10 rows
tail(world_population, n=10)
```

# 3.  Duplicate rows
#       * duplicated() returns TRUE for each row that is an exact copy of an             earlier row. Summing those TRUEs counts the duplicates, because TRUE           counts as 1.
#        * distinct() (from dplyr) keeps only unique rows

```{r}
# Count fully duplicated rows
duplicate_count <- sum(duplicated(world_population))
cat("Duplicated rows found: ", duplicate_count, "\n")

# Keep only unique rows (does nothing if the count above is 0)
world_population <- distinct(world_population)

# Confirm the new shape
dim(world_population)
```

# 4.  Missing values
#       is.na() marks each cell TRUE if it is missing. colSums() adds them up          for each column.

```{r}
# Number of NA values in each column
missing_per_column <- colSums(is.na(world_population))
missing_per_column

# Number of empty-string cells in each text column
blank_per_column <- sapply(world_population, function(column) sum(column == "", na.rm = TRUE))
blank_per_column
```
# 5.   Select the quantitative (measured) measured

```{r}
# Keep only the quantitative (measured) columns; Rank is an ordering label, not a measurement
quantitative_data <- worl_population %>%
  select(where(is.numeric), -Rank)

names(quantitative_data)
```
# 6. Box plots
```{r}
# Reshape from wide (one column per variable) to long (variable, value)
population_long <- quantitative_data %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(),
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value")

# One box plot per variable, each with its own y-axis
ggplot(population_long, aes(x = "", y=value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill="steelblue", outlier.colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Box plots of quantitative variables",
       x = NULL, y = "Value") +
  theme_minimal()
```
# 7.  Count the outliers

```{r}
# Count values outside the 1.5 IQR fences for one numeric vector
count_outliers <- function(x){
  quartiles <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr_value <- quartiles[2] - quartiles[1]
  lower_fence <- quartiles[1] - 1.5 * iqr_value
  upper_fence <- quartiles[2] + 1.5 * iqr_value
  sum(x < lower_fence | x > upper_fence, na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Apply to every quantitative column
sapply(quantitative_data, count_outliers)
```
# 8.  See who the outliers are

```{r}
# The ten largest populations in 2022
world_population %>%
  arrange(desc(`2022 Population`)) %>%
  select(`Country/Territory`, `2022 Population`, `Area (km`, `Density (per km2)`) %>%
  head(10)
```
